title: Can We Ditch BMI for an Obesity Index That Predicts Disease Risk Better? - Nautilus
gist: A Science Bulletin study of 4.26 million Chinese adults compared 15 obesity indices and found different indices best predict different diseases, so no single measure captures obesity risk. BMI's simplicity and inertia mean it likely persists.

insights.claim: BMI uses only height and weight and ignores fat distribution and muscle mass, but its simplicity and nearly two-century history explain why it persists.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Expect clinical and insurance practice to keep relying on BMI despite its flaws.
insights.locator: As far as obesity measures go

insights.claim: A study of 4,258,033 adults aged 35 to 75 from the ChinaHEART cohort compared 15 obesity indices across body shape, visceral fat and metabolic function groups.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Large-sample evidence base for index comparisons.

insights.claim: The Chinese visceral adiposity index best predicted cardiovascular disease risk, the triglyceride-glucose index best predicted diabetes risk, and a body shape index best predicted COPD risk.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Disease-specific risk scoring could favor targeted metabolic and visceral fat measures over BMI.
insights.locator: For example, the Chinese visceral adiposity index

insights.claim: None of the 15 obesity metrics showed a strong association with cancer, and some indices showed nonlinear or inverse associations with COPD and cancer.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Obesity-based screening may be weak for cancer risk stratification.

insights.claim: Relationships found were moderate at best and the cohort was all mainland Chinese, so results may not apply to other ethnicities.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Discount generalization to Western populations until replicated.
insights.locator: Because the cohort members were all from mainland China
